claim: Bacteriophages were discovered by D'Herelle in 1917 and Twort in 1915.
source: Following the discovery of bacteriophages (D'Herelle, 1917; Twort, 1915)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to D'Herelle (1917) and Twort (1915).

claim: E. coli's T1 through T7 phages were widely accepted as model systems.
source: Escherichia coli's T1 through T7 phages were widely accepted as model systems (Keen, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Keen (2015).

claim: T-even phages were used to determine mutation manifestation at the molecular level, gene topology, and that nucleic acids are decoded in triplets.
source: T-even phages were used to determine mutation manifestation at the molecular level, gene topology, and that fact that nucleic acids are decoded in triplets (Benzer, 1961; Crick et al., 1961).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Benzer (1961) and Crick et al. (1961).

claim: Rapid lysing T-even mutants (r mutants) produce plaques with clear edges while wild type T-even phages have fuzzy edges.
source: Early geneticists observed an interesting phenotype in rapid lysing T-even mutants, called r mutants, which produce plaques with clear edges while plaques of wild type (WT; all acronyms are expanded in Table 1) T-even phages have fuzzy edges (Hershey, 1946; Paddison et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hershey (1946) and Paddison et al. (1998).

claim: Edge fuzziness in T-even phage plaques is the consequence of inhibited cell lysis triggered by the adsorption of additional phage after initial infection.
source: Edge fuzziness is the consequence of inhibited cell lysis triggered by the adsorption of additional phage after initial infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about lysis inhibition.

claim: Superinfection stabilizes infected cells as measured by optical density.
source: This 'superinfection' also stabilizes infected cells as measured by optical density (Doermann, 1948).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Doermann (1948).

claim: Lysis inhibition allows for prolonged production of progeny phage resulting in larger phage bursts.
source: The phenomenon, termed lysis inhibition (LIN), is significant for two reasons (Figure 1A and B): it allows for prolonged production of progeny phage resulting in larger phage bursts
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abedon (1990, 2019) and Doermann (1948).

claim: Lysis inhibition protects progeny phage from adsorbing to infected cells, which are not productive hosts for secondarily adsorbed phages.
source: it protects progeny phage from adsorbing to infected cells, which are not productive hosts for secondarily adsorbed phages (Abedon, 1990; Abedon, 2019; Doermann, 1948).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abedon (1990, 2019) and Doermann (1948).

claim: Lysis inhibition is considered an important adaptation in environments where host bacteria are scarce but free virions are plentiful.
source: Consequently, LIN is considered an important adaptation in environments where host bacteria are scarce but free virions are plentiful (Abedon, 1990; Abedon, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abedon (1990, 2019).

claim: Lysis inhibition has only been well characterized in T-even coliphages where it is mediated by holins and antiholins.
source: Despite being discovered over half a century ago, LIN has only been well characterized in T-even coliphages where it is mediated by holins and antiholins (Chen and Young, 2016; Paddison et al., 1998; Ramanculov and Young, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen and Young (2016), Paddison et al. (1998), and Ramanculov and Young (2001).

claim: Holins are the first step in canonical holin-endolysin-spanin lysis systems in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Holins are the first step in canonical holin-endolysin-spanin lysis systems in Gram-negative bacteria (Cahill and Young, 2019; Young, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cahill and Young (2019) and Young (2014).

claim: Holins accumulate in the inner membrane until they trigger, making holes that enable endolysin digestion of the peptidoglycan after which spanins fuse the inner and outer membranes to complete cell lysis.
source: Holins accumulate in the inner membrane until they trigger, making holes that enable endolysin digestion of the peptidoglycan after which spanins fuse the inner and outer membranes to complete cell lysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about phage lysis mechanisms.

claim: During lysis inhibition, antiholins inhibit holin triggering thereby stopping the progression towards lysis.
source: During lysis inhibition, antiholins inhibit holin triggering thereby stopping the progression towards lysis (Chen and Young, 2016; Paddison et al., 1998; Ramanculov and Young, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen and Young (2016), Paddison et al. (1998), and Ramanculov and Young (2001).

claim: ICP1 completes virion production within 20-25 minutes in PLE (-) V. cholerae after infection at low multiplicity of infection (MOI = 0.1).
source: After infection at low multiplicity of infection (MOI; MOI = 0.1), ICP1 completes virion production within 20–25 minutes in PLE (-) V. cholerae (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Hara et al. (2017).

claim: 90 minutes pass before visible lysis of PLE (-) V. cholerae infected at high MOI (MOI = 5).
source: This timeframe is markedly abbreviated with respect to the 90 minutes that pass before visible lysis of the same host infected at a high MOI (MOI = 5) (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Hara et al. (2017).

claim: When infecting PLE (-) V. cholerae with ICP1 at MOI = 1, an early lysis event occurs 20 minutes post-infection after which the optical density of the culture stabilizes.
source: When infecting PLE (-) V. cholerae with ICP1 at MOI = 1, we observed an early lysis event 20 minutes post-infection after which the optical density of the culture stabilized (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Superinfection of PLE (-) V. cholerae with ICP1 (MOI = 1 followed by MOSI = 5) stabilizes the culture optical density, eliminating the early lysis event.
source: To determine whether superinfection by ICP1 of PLE (-) V. cholerae shares this characteristic, we infected cultures with ICP1 (MOI = 1), let phage adsorb for four minutes, then superinfected the culture with ICP1 (multiplicity of superinfection; MOSI = 5). As expected of a phage exhibiting LIN, the culture optical density was stabilized, eliminating the early lysis event (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) collapses the proton motive force and disrupts lysis inhibition by T-even phages, causing rapid lysis of infected E. coli.
source: One such poison, the ionophore 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), collapses the proton motive force and subsequently disrupts LIN by T-even phages, causing rapid lysis of infected E. coli (Abedon, 1992; Heagy, 1950).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abedon (1992) and Heagy (1950).

claim: Exposure of PLE (-) V. cholerae infected at high MOI (MOI = 5) to 2,4-dinitrophenol results in a crash in optical density.
source: To test if ICP1 LIN is similarly linked to proton motive force, we exposed PLE (-) V. cholerae infected at a high MOI (MOI = 5) to 2,4-dinitrophenol (Figure 1D) and observed the expected crash in optical density
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ICP1 exhibits lysis inhibition in V. cholerae.
source: further supporting the conclusion that ICP1 exhibits LIN in V. cholerae.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental observations including optical density stabilization, superinfection effects, and DNP sensitivity.

claim: Holins contain at least one transmembrane domain.
source: Holins are diverse proteins, however, they all include at least one transmembrane domain (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al. (2000).

claim: Three candidate gene products (Gp137-Gp139) in ICP1 contain predicted transmembrane domains and are conserved in previously analyzed ICP1 isolates.
source: As a result we narrowed our search to gene products containing a predicted transmembrane domain that were conserved in previously analyzed ICP1 isolates (Angermeyer et al., 2018) leaving us with three candidate gene products: Gp137-Gp139 (Figure 2B; further described in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis and reference to Angermeyer et al. (2018), with data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ICP1 Gp137 contains the DUF3154 Pfam (reclassified as GTA_holin_3TM).
source: Analysis of these proteins using remote homology and synteny via Phagonaute identified the DUF3154 Pfam (reclassified as GTA_holin_3TM (PF11351); Delattre et al., 2016; El-Gebali et al., 2019; Sonnhammer et al., 1997) in ICP1 Gp137
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis and citations to Delattre et al. (2016), El-Gebali et al. (2019), and Sonnhammer et al. (1997).

claim: ICP1 Gp137 was named TeaA for its T-holin-esque activity.
source: which we have since named TeaA.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Canonical holins including T4's T-holin accumulate in the membrane until they collapse the proton motive force and form pores or are triggered by an energy poison.
source: In E. coli, canonical holins including T4's T-holin, accumulate in the membrane until they collapse the proton motive force and form pores or are triggered by an energy poison.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about holin function.

claim: Premature holin triggering results in loss of viability and commits the cell to eventual lysis, decreasing the optical density.
source: Premature holin triggering results in loss of viability and commits the cell to eventual lysis, decreasing the optical density (Garrett and Young, 1982; Josslin, 1971).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Garrett and Young (1982) and Josslin (1971).

claim: Upon induction, T-holinT4 and TeaA decreased the red fluorescence of DiOC2(3), consistent with holin activity.
source: Upon induction, T-holinT4 and TeaA decreased the red fluorescence, consistent with holin activity, while the empty vector (EV) did not (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TeaA causes rapid decrease in optical density after 2,4-dinitrophenol addition, comparable to T-holinT4.
source: Holin activity by TeaA was further demonstrated by the rapid decrease in optical density after 2,4-dinitrophenol addition which was comparable to the decrease in optical density observed with T-holinT4 expressing V. cholerae after 2,4-dinitrophenol treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The holin TT4 or TeaA alone is enough to lyse V. cholerae under laboratory conditions.
source: Interestingly, though endolysin activity is described as necessary in holin-endolysin-spanin systems (Young, 2014), the holin TT4 or TeaA alone is enough to lyse V. cholerae under laboratory conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and contrasts with established knowledge cited from Young (2014).

claim: Antiholins can interact with holins within the inner membrane, periplasm, or cytoplasm.
source: Antiholins can interact with holins within the inner membrane (Moussa et al., 2012; Young, 2013), periplasm (Tran et al., 2005), or cytoplasm (Chen and Young, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moussa et al. (2012), Young (2013), Tran et al. (2005), and Chen and Young (2016).

claim: Previously characterized periplasmic antiholins contain transmembrane domains for tethering to the membrane and subsequent release into the periplasm.
source: previously characterized periplasmic antiholins contain transmembrane domains for tethering to the membrane and subsequent release into the periplasm (Tran et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tran et al. (2007).

claim: Antiholins are often found near holin genes, in many cases utilizing an alternative start site within the holin sequence or occupying an overlapping open reading frame.
source: Antiholins are often found near holin genes, in many cases utilizing an alternative start site within the holin sequence or occupying an overlapping open reading frame (Bläsi and Young, 1996; Graschopf and Bläsi, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bläsi and Young (1996) and Graschopf and Bläsi (1999).

claim: ICP1 Gp138 was named ArrA as a potential antiholin.
source: With these data in mind, we began to investigate Gp138, which we subsequently named ArrA, as a potential antiholin (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: T4 antiholins RIT4 and RIIIT4 were initially identified when mutations in these genes demonstrated a rapid lysis plaque morphology.
source: The T4 antiholins, RIT4 and RIIIT4 were initially identified when mutations in these genes demonstrated a rapid lysis plaque morphology.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about T4 antiholins.

claim: Phages lacking functional antiholins form plaques with sharply defined edges because lysis inhibition no longer occurs.
source: Phages lacking functional antiholins form plaques with sharply defined edges because lysis inhibition no longer occurs.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about antiholin function.

claim: ICP1 challenged with CRISPR-Cas (+) V. cholerae containing a spacer targeting arrA produced clear-edged plaques.
source: In an effort to find similar rapid-lysing ICP1 mutants with antiholin modifications, we challenged ICP1 with CRISPR-Cas (+) V. cholerae containing a spacer targeting arrA. We observed a mixture of edge phenotypes including clear-edged plaques (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expressing ArrA in trans recovered the fuzzy-edged plaque phenotype in ICP1 arrA mutants.
source: and recovered the fuzzy-edged phenotype by expressing ArrA in trans (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ΔarrA ICP1 forms plaques that have clear edges.
source: In support of ArrA acting as an antiholin whose absence results in rapid lysis, ΔarrA ICP1 forms plaques that have clear edges (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: arrA is not an essential gene despite its conservation.
source: Of note, and consistent with arrA acting as an antiholin, we successfully constructed an arrA knockout demonstrating that, despite its conservation, arrA is not an essential gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing successful construction of an arrA knockout.

claim: ΔarrA ICP1 causes rapid lysis once lysis begins, in contrast to the more prolonged decline seen in wild type infections exhibiting LIN.
source: Attempts to obtain high titer stocks of ΔarrA ICP1 were unsuccessful (consistent with decreased phage yields) hindering tests of infection at high multiplicities of infection. Instead, we infected PLE (-) V. cholerae with ΔarrA ICP1, waited for approximately two cycles of infection to complete, and then, once lysis began, we observed a rapid crash in optical density (Figure 3D). Such kinetics are in stark contrast to the more prolonged decline seen in wild type infections exhibiting LIN (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and comparison to Figure 1C.

claim: Supplying ArrA in trans recovered lysis kinetics characteristic of LIN in which the optical density was stabilized for 30 additional minutes before the culture cleared.
source: To be sure this was due to ArrA, we supplied ArrA in trans and recovered lysis kinetics characteristic of LIN in which the optical density was stabilized for 30 additional minutes before the culture cleared (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Exposure of cultures with ArrA supplied in trans to 2,4-dinitrophenol collapses the culture, confirming stabilization was accomplished through LIN.
source: To further test that this stabilization of optical density by ArrA when supplied in trans was accomplished through LIN, we exposed cultures to 2,4-dinitrophenol disrupting the proton motive force and collapsing the culture (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ArrA is an ICP1-encoded antiholin that helps regulate lysis timing.
source: These data support the conclusion that ArrA is an ICP1-encoded antiholin that helps regulate lysis timing.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental observations including plaque morphology, lysis kinetics, and complementation experiments.

claim: BLASTP analysis of TeaA revealed homologs present throughout marine phage and bacterial genomes.
source: BLASTP analysis of TeaA revealed homologs present throughout marine phage and bacterial genomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Some organisms containing TeaA homologs also contain ArrA homologs, though these were limited to vibriophages.
source: ArrA yielded fewer homologs than TeaA (Supplementary file 3), however, using less stringent search parameters, we found that some organisms containing TeaA homologs also contain ArrA homologs, though these were limited to vibriophages (Figure 3E and Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3E and Supplementary files 2 and 3.

claim: There are potential homologous LIN systems - complete with both holin and antiholin - present in phages other than ICP1.
source: This suggests that there are potential homologous LIN systems - complete with both holin and antiholin - present in phages other than ICP1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the bioinformatic analysis showing co-occurrence of TeaA and ArrA homologs.

claim: ICP1 infection of PLE (-) V. cholerae at high MOI (MOI = 5) gradually lyses cultures reaching the lowest optical density ~90 minutes after infection.
source: Consistent with previous experiments at high MOI (MOI = 5) (O'Hara et al., 2017), ICP1 infection of PLE (-) V. cholerae gradually lyses cultures reaching the lowest optical density ~90 minutes after infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data consistent with O'Hara et al. (2017).

claim: Upon infection of PLE 1 V. cholerae, rapid lysis starts 20 minutes post-infection.
source: In contrast, upon infection of PLE 1 V. cholerae, rapid lysis starts 20 minutes post-infection (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The earliest known PLEs (PLEs 4 and 5) contain two ORFs with predicted transmembrane domains: ORF2 and ORF26.
source: However, the earliest known PLEs, (PLEs 4 and 5) contain two ORFs with predicted transmembrane domains: ORF2 and ORF26.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of PLE sequences.

claim: ORF2PLE 4/5 does not have homologs in PLEs 1 or 2.
source: ORF2PLE 4/5 does not have homologs in PLEs 1 or 2, suggesting it is not a conserved player mediating accelerated lysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of PLE sequences.

claim: PLEs 1, 2, and 3 contain previously unannotated open reading frames (ORF20.1PLE 1, ORF24.1PLE 2 and ORF24.1PLE 3) that are homologous to ORF26PLE 4/5 and contain transmembrane domains.
source: Although no homologs were immediately obvious, the synteny between PLEs suggested the presence of previously unannotated open reading frames in PLEs 1, 2, and 3 (namely ORF20.1PLE 1, ORF24.1PLE 2 and ORF24.1PLE 3), which are homologous to ORF26PLE 4/5 and contain transmembrane domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of PLE sequences.

claim: These ORFs were named lidI and the homologs cluster into two groups: lidIPLE 1 and lidIPLE 2 encode for a 66 amino acid long protein, while lidIPLE 3, lidIPLE 4 and lidIPLE 5 encode larger proteins at 121 amino acids.
source: We subsequently named these genes lidI and the homologs cluster into two groups: lidIPLE 1 and lidIPLE 2 encode for a 66 amino acid long protein, while lidIPLE 3, lidIPLE 4 and lidIPLE 5 encode larger proteins at 121 amino acids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: LidI ORFs have no significant homology to other genes or predicted functional domains beyond their shared transmembrane domains.
source: These ORFs have no significant homology to other genes or predicted functional domains beyond their shared transmembrane domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis.

claim: FLAG-LidIPLE 1 is not visualizable in the absence of phage infection.
source: We could not visualize FLAG-LidIPLE 1 in the absence of phage infection
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data.

claim: When infected by ICP1 at MOI = 2, FLAG-LidIPLE 1 is detectable by Western blot late in infection – 18 to 20 minutes post phage addition and immediately prior to the sudden decrease in OD characteristic of PLE-mediated accelerated lysis.
source: however, when infected by ICP1 at MOI = 2, FLAG-LidIPLE 1 was detectable by Western blot late in infection – 18 to 20 minutes post phage addition and immediately prior to the sudden decrease in OD characteristic of PLE-mediated accelerated lysis (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: LidIPLE 1 is sufficient to recapitulate the PLE-mediated accelerated lysis phenotype during ICP1 infection.
source: After confirming lidIPLE 1 expression during ICP1 infection, we next sought to characterize LidIPLE 1 function in PLE (-) V. cholerae. During infection with ICP1, LidIPLE 1 was sufficient to recapitulate the PLE-mediated accelerated lysis phenotype (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of LidIPLE 1 at the same level of induction in the absence of phage does not alter cellular proton motive force or make cells susceptible to 2,4-dinitrophenol induced lysis.
source: This phenotype is consistent with lidIPLE 1 encoding a holin; however, expression of LidIPLE 1 at the same level of induction in the absence of phage did not alter cellular proton motive force or make cells susceptible to 2,4-dinitrophenol induced lysis (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: LidIPLE 1's ability to mediate cell lysis is dependent on the presence of ICP1.
source: These data suggest that LidIPLE 1 does not act as a canonical holin when expressed alone and that its ability to mediate cell lysis is dependent on the presence of ICP1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing LidI requires ICP1 for lysis activity.

claim: Deletion of lidIPLE 1 from PLE 1 V. cholerae does not change lysis kinetics.
source: Interestingly, however, when we deleted lidIPLE 1 from PLE 1 V. cholerae the lysis kinetics were unchanged (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PLE 1 and PLE 1 ΔlidI strains both demonstrate accelerated lysis when exogenous phage is added.
source: To be sure the accelerated lysis is not the consequence of PLE inhibiting the production of phage that are necessary to superinfect cells, exogenous phage was added to PLE 1 and PLE 1 ΔlidI strains both of which still demonstrated accelerated lysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: LidIPLE 4 is sufficient to cause accelerated lysis in the absence of PLE.
source: As these findings were at odds with the conservation of lidI homologs in all the known PLEs, we tested a representative of the other cluster of homologs, LidIPLE 4, for conserved function. Indeed, LidIPLE 4 is sufficient to cause accelerated lysis in the absence of PLE
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: LidIPLE 4 is not necessary for accelerated lysis - PLE 4 ΔlidI V. cholerae strains still exhibit accelerated lysis.
source: however again we found that it is not necessary – PLE 4 ΔlidI V. cholerae strains still exhibit accelerated lysis (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PLE 1 mutants containing a single knockout of each individual open reading frame all demonstrated accelerated lysis when exposed to phage.
source: To further investigate the role of individual genes in lysis timing, PLE 1 mutants containing a single knockout of each individual open reading frame were exposed to phage and each demonstrated accelerated lysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: No other single PLE 1 ORF expressed individually was sufficient to recapitulate PLE-mediated accelerated lysis.
source: To identify other PLE-encoded factors sufficient to recapitulate PLE-mediated accelerated lysis, we expressed each PLE 1 ORF individually and challenged those strains with phage. This screen did not identify any other single genes sufficient to accelerate lysis
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental screening data.

claim: PLE mediated accelerated cell lysis is the consequence of the activity of two or more functionally redundant gene products, of which LidI is the only product sufficient to phenocopy the PLE-encoded phenotype.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that PLE mediated accelerated cell lysis is the consequence of the activity of two or more functionally redundant gene products, of which LidI is the only product sufficient to phenocopy the PLE-encoded phenotype.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing LidI sufficiency but not necessity, and lack of other single sufficient genes.

claim: No single PLE open reading frame is necessary for inhibition of ICP1 plaque formation.
source: Although redundancy is perhaps not expected for mobile genetic elements (MGEs) with restricted genome size, we have additionally observed that no single PLE open reading frame is necessary for inhibition of ICP1 plaque formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Multiple strategies act synergistically to eliminate phage production in addition to accelerating lysis.
source: suggesting that multiple strategies act synergistically to eliminate phage production in addition to accelerating lysis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that no single gene is necessary for PLE's anti-phage activity.

claim: LidIPLE 1-mediated accelerated lysis timing is dependent on MOI, with up to a 40 minutes delay at the lowest MOI.
source: This is evidenced by the stabilization of culture optical density until complete lysis ~90 minutes in PLE (-) V. cholerae infected at various multiplicities of infection (Figure 5A). The differential onset of LIN means that accelerated lysis mediated by LidIPLE 1 would also be expected to change in accordance with MOI if it functions by disrupting LIN. Indeed, we observed differential lysis timing dependent on the MOI in cultures expressing LidIPLE 1 with up to a 40 minutes delay at the lowest MOI (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: LidIPLE 1 functions through lysis inhibition disruption.
source: suggesting that LidIPLE 1 functions through lysis inhibition disruption.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MOI-dependent lysis timing data.

claim: lidIPLE 1 expression in PLE (-) V. cholerae does not change the efficiency of plaquing (EOP) by ICP1.
source: Congruent with LidIPLE 1 disrupting LIN, lidIPLE 1 expression in PLE (-) V. cholerae does not change the efficiency of plaquing (EOP) by ICP1, an experiment that probes the number of successful initial infections at a low multiplicity of infection (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PLE (-) V. cholerae expressing lidIPLE 1 in trans shows loss of fuzzy plaque edges.
source: Consistent with this, the phenotypic change in plaque morphology expected of disrupted LIN is the loss of fuzzy plaque edges, which we see in PLE (-) V. cholerae expressing lidIPLE 1 in trans (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Induction of lidIPLE 1 at the time of infection or 20 minutes before infection resulted in decreased phage yield by one or two orders of magnitude, respectively, in comparison to strains with the empty vector control.
source: To determine if LidIPLE 1 alone can impact the number of phage produced from an infection, expression was induced prior to, at the time of, and at various intervals after infection with ICP1 at a high MOI (MOI = 5). Induction of lidIPLE 1 at the time of infection or 20 minutes before infection resulted in decreased phage yield by one or two orders of magnitude, respectively, in comparison to strains with the empty vector control (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: LidIPLE 4 shows the same decreased phage yield as LidIPLE 1.
source: Not only did we find this to be true of LidIPLE 1, but we also tested the LidIPLE 4 homolog for conserved inhibition of ICP1 and observed the same decreased phage yield (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When infections start out with a low number of phage per cell (MOI ≤0.001), there is still accelerated lysis and decreased progeny phage production when LidIPLE 1 expression is induced.
source: Subsequent testing revealed that when infections start out with a low number of phage per cell (MOI ≤0.001), there is still accelerated lysis and decreased progeny phage production when LidIPLE 1 expression is induced (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: LidI is the first PLE-encoded ORF that can singlehandedly negatively impact ICP1 phage yield.
source: These data reveal LidI as the first PLE-encoded ORF that can singlehandedly negatively impact ICP1 phage yield.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased phage yield with LidI expression.

claim: For each spacer tested, fewer phage progeny from lidIPLE 1 V. cholerae were able to overcome CRISPR-Cas targeting than progeny from infections of strains without lidIPLE 1.
source: For each spacer, fewer phage progeny from lidIPLE 1 V. cholerae were able to overcome targeting than progeny from infections of strains without lidIPLE 1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The defect in overcoming CRISPR-Cas targeting is due to the LidI-mediated decrease in the population of phages as the frequency of phage escaping stays the same.
source: This defect is due to the LidI-mediated decrease in the population of phages as the frequency of phage escaping stays the same (e.g. ~2 out of every thousand phages can overcome spacer C, Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Because less phage are produced from lidIPLE 1-expressing V. cholerae, an order of magnitude fewer phages can overcome the spacer in the population.
source: Consequently, because less phage are produced from lidIPLE 1-expressing V. cholerae, an order of magnitude fewer phages can overcome the spacer in the population (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The presence of LidIPLE 1 decreased the number of progeny phages per infection that recombined to reconstitute the CRISPR-Cas system and overcome PLE.
source: Predictably, the presence of LidIPLE 1 decreased the number of progeny phages per infection that recombined to reconstitute the CRISPR-Cas system and overcome PLE (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: LidI imposes a bottleneck on ICP1's population size resulting in fewer diverse phages and limiting ICP1's potential to escape anti-phage activity.
source: Although LidI expression does not directly impact ICP1 evolvability within infected cells, these data demonstrate that LidI imposes a bottleneck on ICP1's population size resulting in fewer diverse phages and limiting ICP1's potential to escape anti-phage activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing decreased phage populations and reduced escape from CRISPR-Cas and PLE.

claim: This work identifies the ICP1-encoded holin, teaA, and antiholin, arrA, that mediate lysis inhibition.
source: This work identifies the ICP1-encoded holin, teaA, and antiholin, arrA, that mediate lysis inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental characterization of TeaA and ArrA.

claim: A conserved PLE protein, LidI, is sufficient to limit the phage produced from infection, bottlenecking ICP1.
source: Through lysis inhibition disruption a conserved PLE protein, LidI, is sufficient to limit the phage produced from infection, bottlenecking ICP1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased phage yield and evolutionary bottleneck.

claim: V. cholerae poses a substantial global health burden as the causative agent of the diarrheal disease cholera.
source: V. cholerae poses a substantial global health burden as the causative agent of the diarrheal disease cholera (Ali et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ali et al. (2015).

claim: In both aquatic reservoirs and stool samples from cholera patients, V. cholerae co-occurs with predatory phages.
source: In both aquatic reservoirs and stool samples from cholera patients, V. cholerae co-occurs with predatory phages.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about V. cholerae ecology.

claim: Several studies have implicated V. cholerae phages in playing a role in modulating cholera outbreaks.
source: Several studies have implicated V. cholerae phages in playing a role in modulating cholera outbreaks (D'Herelle and Malone, 1927; Faruque et al., 2005a; Faruque et al., 2005b; Jensen et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to D'Herelle and Malone (1927), Faruque et al. (2005a, 2005b), and Jensen et al. (2006).

claim: Phage cocktails have been proposed as prophylactics to curb cholera transmission.
source: leading to proposals of phage cocktails as prophylactics to curb cholera transmission (Yen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yen et al. (2017).

claim: The predominant phage in cholera patient samples is ICP1, a lytic myovirus.
source: The predominant phage in cholera patient samples is ICP1, a lytic myovirus (Seed et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Seed et al. (2011).

claim: ICP1 is locked in a dynamic arms race with V. cholerae with no clear winner as both continue to be isolated from patients in the cholera endemic region of Bangladesh.
source: that is locked in a dynamic arms race with no clear winner as both V. cholerae and ICP1 continue to be isolated from patients in the cholera endemic region of Bangladesh (Angermeyer et al., 2018; McKitterick et al., 2019a; McKitterick et al., 2019a; Seed et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Angermeyer et al. (2018), McKitterick et al. (2019a), and Seed et al. (2011).

claim: PLE is a parasitic phage satellite found integrated in the chromosome of clinical V. cholerae isolates.
source: Added into the evolutionary fray is a parasitic phage satellite called PLE (phage-inducible chromosomal island-like element) found integrated in the chromosome of clinical V. cholerae isolates (McKitterick et al., 2019b; O'Hara et al., 2017; Seed et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McKitterick et al. (2019b), O'Hara et al. (2017), and Seed et al. (2013).

claim: Previous analysis of isolates dating back to 1949 revealed a succession of five distinct PLEs (PLE 1 through PLE 5) in V. cholerae which possess shared genomic architecture.
source: Previous analysis of isolates dating back to 1949 revealed a succession of five distinct PLEs (PLE 1 through PLE 5 of which PLE 1 is the most recently circulating PLE) in V. cholerae which possess shared genomic architecture.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about PLE evolution.

claim: Each PLE provides V. cholerae with a clear fitness benefit in the defense against ICP1 as PLE abolishes phage production.
source: Each PLE provides V. cholerae with a clear fitness benefit in the defense against ICP1 as PLE abolishes phage production (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Hara et al. (2017).

claim: Upon infection, PLE excises from the bacterial chromosome, harnessing an ICP1-encoded protein as the trigger.
source: Upon infection, PLE excises from the bacterial chromosome, harnessing an ICP1-encoded protein as the trigger (McKitterick and Seed, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McKitterick and Seed (2018).

claim: PLE replicates using both PLE and ICP1-encoded products.
source: replicates using both PLE and ICP1-encoded products (Barth et al., 2020; McKitterick et al., 2019a)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barth et al. (2020) and McKitterick et al. (2019a).

claim: PLE accelerates cell lysis after forming particles hypothesized to be made by hijacking ICP1 structural components to transduce the PLE genome to naïve recipient cells.
source: and accelerates cell lysis after forming particles hypothesized to be made by hijacking ICP1 structural components to transduce the PLE genome to naïve recipient cells (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Hara et al. (2017) and involves speculation about particle formation.

claim: As no infectious ICP1 are produced, PLE defends populations of V. cholerae from ICP1 attack, functioning as an abortive infection system.
source: As no infectious ICP1 are produced, PLE defends populations of V. cholerae from ICP1 attack, functioning as an abortive infection system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PLE abolishes ICP1 production.

claim: ICP1 acquired a Type I-F CRISPR-Cas system to target PLE in a sequence-specific manner, restoring ICP1 progeny phage production and overcoming PLE.
source: In the face of this anti-phage element, ICP1 acquired a Type I-F CRISPR-Cas system to target PLE in a sequence-specific manner, restoring ICP1 progeny phage production and overcoming PLE (McKitterick et al., 2019b; Seed et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McKitterick et al. (2019b) and Seed et al. (2013).

claim: Efforts to understand how PLEs restrict ICP1 have yet to identify any single PLE open reading frame necessary for inhibition.
source: While the full extent of ICP1, PLE, and V. cholerae interactions are unknown and continuing to evolve, efforts to understand how PLEs restrict ICP1 have yet to identify any single PLE open reading frame necessary for inhibition (via testing of PLE-encoded repA, which is necessary for PLE replication [Barth et al., 2020] and int, which is required for PLE excision [McKitterick and Seed, 2018]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barth et al. (2020) and McKitterick and Seed (2018).

claim: PLE requires phage-encoded products, consequently depending on ICP1 for horizontal transmission.
source: From the only characterized processes, namely excision and replication, it is clear that PLE requires phage-encoded products, consequently depending on ICP1 for horizontal transmission
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PLE uses ICP1-encoded products for excision and replication.

claim: PLE completely abolishes ICP1 production, which is uncharacteristic of other phage satellites like SaPIs which decrease but do not eliminate the production of progeny virions.
source: however, uncharacteristic of other phage satellites like the well characterized Staphylococcus aureus pathogenicity islands (SaPIs) which decrease but do not eliminate the production of progeny virions, PLE completely abolishes ICP1 production
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to established knowledge about SaPIs.

claim: The cyclic-oligonucleotide-based anti-phage signaling system is found on MGEs in bacteria including V. cholerae, and in E. coli serves as an abortive infection system upon phage infection and can cause lysis on an accelerated timescale.
source: One recently discovered example of how prevalent these confounding factors are is that of the cyclic-oligonucleotide-based anti-phage signaling system, which is found on MGEs in bacteria including V. cholerae, and that, in E. coli, serves as an abortive infection system upon phage infection and can cause lysis on an accelerated timescale (Cohen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cohen et al. (2019).
